HATE SPEECH - THE FINE LINE

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
where do we draw the line between free speech and hate speech and what should the penalties be

Unique Selling Point:
TOPICAL NEWS OF THE WEEK - NEEDING GREATER ANALYSIS

Further information:
MONDAY - Julius Malema appeared in the Bloemfontein Magistrates Court on a charge of breaking the Riotous Assemblies Act after telling people to invade empty land - This was in relation to a speech he made at the EFF’s national people’s assembly at the University of the Free State on December 16, 2014. He urged supporters to occupy unoccupied land, a statement made in line with one of the party’s seven cardinal pillars. AFRIFORUM LAID CHARGES. On Monday the case was postponed pending Malema challenging the validity of the charges constitutionally - but he stepped outside and uttered the same rhetoric to the crowds again.

Is this free speech or hate speech and what impact will the new Prevention and Combatting of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Bill have on people who claim to speak their minds but are crossing the hate speech lines.

We speak to a constitutional law / freedom of expression expert - Victoria Bronstein; an Editor - hopefully The City Press's Mondli Makhanya; The Justice Department about the new bill and how it is different and then the Freedom of Expression Institute's Tusi Fokane (if she bails we'll find another representative analyst)

Mr. John Vlismas
Ms. Tusi Fokane EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR
Prof. VICTORIA BRONSTEIN
Mr. JOHN JEFFERY DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE

Press Release:


Hate Speech: The Fine Line
Julius Malema recently appeared before the courts on charges of contravening the riotous assemblies act, linked to his public call for people to invade vacant land back in 2014. He’s challenged the charges in the Constitutional Court raising the question of how we should police the fine line between free speech and hate speech. Carte Blanche analyses events that have led to a new bill aimed at preventing and combating hate crimes and hate speech.


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Racial tensions flared up again this week, when an act – perceived by some – as being of racial hatred, came before a court on the one hand…

UPSOOUND: VIDEO CRYING MAN

VO: And on the other, a political leader addressed a crowd, some have said, inciting racial hatred.

UPSOUND VIDEO: “We are not calling for the slaughter of white people, at least for now”

LINK: Free Speech. Hate Speech – one man’s terrorist might be another’s freedom fighter – well, government says it’s time to draw a line with the proposed prevention and combatting of hate speech and hate crimes bill.

DM: It will make it more difficult – people will have to think twice – they can’t just say sorry I didn’t intend it

VO: But the net is cast so wide that it may possibly even have consequences for controversial comedians like John Vlismas.

BONGANI: Possibly jail time?
JOHN: Will it though? This is my big question? Are we really going to in SA with the Bill of Rights that we have – jail people for the use of words?

VO: Well, yes, if the new bill gets passed in it’s current form - transgressors could get between three to 10 years behind bars.

Word on the street is that South Africans are in two minds about the criminalisation of hate speech.

SAKHILE MFEKA : everyone has the right to speak what they have mind
SHANNON SCHMIDT: It’s kind of a double edged sword.
MASECHABA MASAKE: it should be criminalised -
JUSTIN FAVER: People selling drugs, people killing each other– I don’t think you can go to jail for ridiculing someone

VO: But racism appears to still be rampant in our beloved country. In 2016 racism scandals have exploded on social media.

DEPUTY MINISTER: The ease of social media has caused more incidents – has put more pressure on us to do something.

VO: Deputy Minister of Justice, John Jeffery explained, that government feels the current Equality Act is insufficient. John Webb caught up with him at Parliament in Cape Town.

DEPUTY MINISTER: The equality courts are only civil – not criminal – it’s basically a remedy between people – what this is doing it’s criminalising hate crimes and hate speech.

VO: But is this kind of legistlation the remedy we need? The Freedom of Expression Institute’s Tusi Fokane doesn’t believe so.

TUSI: If after 22 years still structural or social issues that have not been effectively dealt with – policing or criminalising hate speech is not going to ensure a more open or a more freer or a more democratic South Africa.

VO: But hate speech isn’t the driving force behind the bill – it was added in this year. The bill has in fact, been in the making for the last 10 years, with the focus being hate crimes says the Deputy Minister.

DEPUTY MINISTER: It makes existing crimes, hate crimes linked to the motive.

VO: The Middleburg Coffin Case would fall into that category – this video shows two white men, Willem Oosthuizen and Theo Martins Jackson, assaulting a black man, Rethabile Mlotshwa, who they accuse of trespassing.

The two men forced, Rethabile into a coffin and then threatened to set it alight with him in it.

UPSOUND: Ek wil die petrol gooi – klim in!

DEPUTY MINISTER: they have been charged with assault GBH – that would become a hate crime if the state can prove that the motive was the race of the person.

JOHN: We have to ask ourselves if hate speech is the same as a hate crime? Do you think anything we say is going to change how those animals think – I don’t think so // that is a crime against humanity – cannot be tolerated.

VO: But when does speaking your mind become hate speech?

Technically Julius Malema’s comment about slaughtering white people - is not hate speech - at least not for now.

TUSI: The interesting thing about Mr. Malema’s comments was being able to side step eminence of whatever it was that he was saying // he said at least for now, based on how he phrased his statement – it would not constitute hate speech.

VO: But still, the country is in turbulent space when it comes to race, hate speech and hate crimes.

68% of all complaints heard by the Human Rights Commission are related to allegations of racial discrimination.

While the new bill aims to address some of these issues, legal minds argue that in it’s current form it is unconstitutional.

Professor Victoria Bronstein specializes in Constitutional Law.

VICTORIA: freedom of expression is crucial for our society, freedom of the media// those are critical for democracy and society and I think this Bill flies in the face of that.

LINK: Freedom of speech is founded on the idea that even if what you are saying makes my blood boil – I will fight to the death for your right to say it – critics say this bill seeks to change that.

BONGANI: We run the risk of policing people’s opinions?
TUSI: You run the risk of criminalising people for making stupid comments or people who make offensive comments or people who make harmful comments and in the environment that we are trying to create, we are trying to create an open democracy – an environment of open dialogue, where every individual’s opinion should be respected

VO: But while Freedom of expression is entrenched in our constitution – it does come with limitations – free speech does not extend itself to propaganda for war, incitement of imminent violence, or the advocacy of hatred based on race, gender, ethnicity or religion that constitutes the incitement to cause harm.

DEPUTY MINISTER: freedom of expression is not a pre-eminent right and it needs to be balanced with other rights, for example the right to dignity. The key issue is going to be defining what hate speech is – so that it doesn’t unduly limit freedom of expression.

VO: Government appears to be aiming for more a sterile, uncontroversial national discourse - while there is a need to interrogate the issues even if it is uncomfortable at times says Professor Bronstein.

VICTORIA: In a democracy, people need to be capable of dealing with offense – you can’t clamp down on all satire – because you’ll end up on protecting a powerful government.

LINK: For critics perhaps the most worries aspect of the bill is that they say it opens the door to censorship and it smacks of authoritarianism.

VO: Even the media could land on the wrong side of the law.

VICTORIA: If Carte Blanche quotes something in order to describe the situation of hate speech, in order to give an example of hate speech – it should be at risk and this bill will make it a risk of being responsible for hate speech

JOHN: The way to generate dialogue is to provoke thought – you can’t provoke thought by being safe – if comedy has to go underground – this will become a cave and we’ll send out videos like any other terrorist organisation

VO: This kind of legislation is not unique to South Africa – over 80 countries have laws addressing hate speech - our lawmakers drew from legislation in Kenya, Canada and Australia.

Professor Bronstein says the Bill could work if it is refined.

VICTORIA: I think that if the Bill clearly prescribed hate speech, hate, speech that incites, then we would have an act that would be workable and that would be valuable in society – but this goes too far and it creates risks.

VO: For government, while the bill may yet be adapted, it is necessary and will be passed.

DM: this bill is not meant to be the panacea for racism - it is a small component against racism and prejudice - as south Africans we need to look at ourselves more closely – tolerate each other, respect each -

OUT TRO
Deadline for public comments extended until 31 January.

PROMOS

PROMO 1 – 15 seconder
VO: A new bill criminalising hurtful and harmful speech might open the door to censorship.

JOHN: Are we really going to in SA with the Bill of Rights that we have – jail people for the use of words? INT1 M4

VO: Where is the line between free speech and hate speech?

PROMO 2

UPSOUND VIDEO: “We are not calling for the slaughter of white people, at least for now”

VO: Is this hate speech or just free speech? Government hopes to draw the line with a new proposed bill – criminalising hate crimes and hate speech.

PROMO 3 – 10 seconder
VO: There’s a fine line between free speech and hate speech - government is calling it with a new proposed bill.

DEPUTY MINISTER: What this is doing it’s criminalising hate crimes and hate speech. INT1 M6
